[given, F2, algebra] ∎

old: 1.1 The map $U:V\to\ell^2$ given by $(Uu)_j=\sqrt{\lambda_j}u_j$ is a surjective isometry, so $V$ is Hilbert and $a$ is its inner product. Since $\lambda_j\ge1$, $a(u,u)\ge\|Ju\|_H^2$, and $a(u,u)=\|u\|_V^2$; hence the form is coercive and bounded. Finite sequences lie in $V$ and are dense in $H$, so $J$ is injective with dense range. [F1, A1, given, algebra]

1.2 Let $B_V:=\{u\in V:\|u\|_V\le1\}$. For any $\varepsilon>0$, choose $N$ so $1/\sqrt{\lambda_{N+1}}<\varepsilon/2$. If $x=Ju$ with $u\in B_V$, then $\sum_{j>N}|x_j|^2=\sum_{j>N}|u_j|^2\le\lambda_{N+1}^{-1}\sum_{j>N}\lambda_j|u_j|^2\le\lambda_{N+1}^{-1}$. The set $C_N:=\{(z_1,\ldots,z_N)\in\mathbb K^N:\sum_{j\le N}\lambda_j|z_j|^2\le1\}$ is closed and bounded in $\mathbb R^N$ (if $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$) or $\mathbb R^{2N}$ (if $\mathbb K=\mathbb C$), so it is compact by Heine--Borel and has a finite $\varepsilon/2$-net with centers in $C_N$. Each center $z$ lifts by zero padding to $\widetilde z=(z_1,\ldots,z_N,0,\ldots)\in J(B_V)$, because its weighted energy is at most one. For $x=Ju\in J(B_V)$, the prefix $(x_1,\ldots,x_N)$ belongs to $C_N$; the net and the tail bound therefore give $\|x-\widetilde z\|_{\ell^2}<\varepsilon$ for one of these finitely many lifts. Thus $J(B_V)$ is totally bounded with centers in itself. Its closure $C:=\overline{J(B_V)}$ is also totally bounded: a finite $\varepsilon/2$-net for $J(B_V)$ is an $\varepsilon$-net for $C$ by the triangle inequality and the definition of closure. The set $C$ is complete because it is closed in the complete Hilbert space $H$: every Cauchy sequence in $C$ converges in $H$, and closedness keeps its limit in $C$. By [F4], $C$ is compact. The unit-ball criterion in [[def-compact-linear-operator]] now shows that $J$ is compact. [F4, F1, given, algebra]

2.1 Apply [F1] at the exact point $(A,b)$. For the matrix edge, $BH\widehat x-A^{-1}Hx=(B-A^{-1})H\widehat x+A^{-1}H(\widehat x-x)$. Since $\|H\|_2\le\|H\|_F$, step 1.1 gives $\eta_A$; the vector edge gives $\eta_b$. Taking Euclidean/Frobenius adjoints yields the stated pullbacks with the same norm discrepancies. 3.1 Fix an output coordinate $j$ of $\widehat\lambda$ and put $q_i=B_{ij}c_i$. By success in [F4] and the relative bound in [F5], $p_i=q_i(1+\alpha_i)$ with $|\alpha_i|\le u$; exact-zero products have $\alpha_i=0$. For each addition $i=2,\ldots,n$, write $s_i=(s_{i-1}+p_i)(1+\beta_i)$ with $|\beta_i|\le u$, taking $\beta_i=0$ when the exact sum is zero. Expanding gives $\widehat\lambda_j=s_n=\sum_{i=1}^n q_i(1+\alpha_i)\prod_{k=\max(2,i)}^n(1+\beta_k)$, with an empty product interpreted as $1$. Each coefficient has at most $n$ factors: for $i=1$ it has one product factor and $n-1$ addition factors, while for $i\ge2$ it has one product factor and $n-i+1$ addition factors. Thus [F6], $nu<1$, and monotonicity of $ku/(1-ku)$ imply that each coefficient differs from $1$ by at most $\gamma_n$. Hence $|\widehat\lambda_j-(B^Tc)_j|\le\gamma_n\sum_i|B_{ij}||c_i|$. Stacking these bounds and applying $\||B|^T|c|\|_2\le\|B\|_F\|c\|_2$ gives $\|\widehat\lambda-B^Tc\|_2\le t\|c\|_2$ and then $\|\widehat\lambda\|_2\le(M+t)\|c\|_2$. Each rounded outer-product entry has error at most $u|\widehat\lambda_i\widehat x_j|$, so its Frobenius error is at most $u(M+t)\|\widehat x\|_2\|c\|_2$. Combining these bounds with step 2.1 gives the stated vector and matrix cotangent estimates. [given, F4, F5, F6, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 For each realized nonzero $c$, any cotangent error vector $z$ is the action on $c$ of the linear map $zc^T/\|c\|^2$, whose induced norm is $\|z\|/\|c\|$; vectorize the matrix cotangent for the matrix edge. When $c=0$, successful operations return exact zero. Thus the realized rounded pullbacks admit local linear-map perturbations with the displayed bounds, without asserting global linearity of rounding. The graph perturbation theorem may propagate these realized maps with exact accumulation. [step 3.1, algebra, construct] ∎

For any partitions $P,Q$, their union is a common refinement, so step 1.1 gives $L(g,P)\le L(g,P\cup Q)\le U(g,P\cup Q)\le U(g,Q)$. Taking the supremum and infimum yields $I_-\le I_+$. If $u,v\in[a,b]$, $|u-v|<\delta$, and $u$ belongs to the neighborhood centered at $x_i$, then both $u$ and $v$ are within $\delta_{x_i}$ of $x_i$. Since $I_-\ge L(g,P)$ and $I_+\le U(g,P)$, we have $0\le I_+-I_-<\varepsilon$. This holds for every $\varepsilon>0$, so $I_-=I_+$. Their common value defines the integral in the statement. Every pair of partitions of these two intervals combines to a partition containing $c$; therefore the infimum of the combined sums is the sum of the two separate infima (choose each sum within $\varepsilon/2$ of its infimum for the reverse inequality). The common upper/lower values from step 2.2 give $\int_a^b g=\int_a^c g+\int_c^b g$. Endpoint cases follow from $\int_a^a g=0$. Reversal is the definition, so the integral is oriented and additive. 2.1 If $N=0$, there are no time steps and the survival-error claim is zero. Suppose $N\ge1$, and put $T_h=N\Delta t>0$. A cohort born with mass $m_0$ and initial age $a_0$ has exact survival mass solving $m'(s)=-\mu(a_0+s)m(s)$; let $q=m_0$ be its reference mass. To apply [F4] at $a_0=0$, define the extension $\bar\mu(r)=\mu(r)$ for $r\ge0$ and $\bar\mu(r)=\mu(0)+\mu'_+(0)r e^r$ for $r<0$. The one-sided derivative $\mu'_+(0)$ exists; the two formulas and their first derivatives match at zero, and $\bar\mu$ and $\bar\mu'$ are bounded on $\mathbb R$. For a cohort whose reference mass is $q>0$, the vector field $f(s,m)=-\bar\mu(a_0+s)m$ is $C^1$ on the open tube $V=(-1,T_h+1)\times(-q,2q)$, where $T_h=N\Delta t$, with all bounds required by [F4] uniform in $a_0$ and proportional to $q$ except for the state-Lipschitz constant, which is bounded by $\|\bar\mu\|_\infty$. The exact continuation $m(s)=m_{\mathrm{start}}\exp(-\int_0^s\bar\mu(a_0+r)\,dr)$ exists on an open interval containing $[0,T_h]$; after shrinking that interval at the endpoints its graph lies in $V$. Its exact forward solution from any $m\in[0,q]$ and its Euler input/output states lie in $K=[0,T_h]\times[0,q]$: mortality is nonnegative for ages $a_0+s\ge0$, and $\Delta t\|\mu\|_\infty\le1$. Thus [F4] gives one-step defect at most $C\Delta t^2q$ and a stability factor $1+L\Delta t$, with constants independent of $a_0$ and proportional to $q$. Applying [L1] on the aligned horizon $T_h=N\Delta t$ gives survival-weight error at most $C_T\Delta t q$ over the full run; the zero-mass case is exact. For the discrete total cohort mass $N_h^k$, positivity and $B_h^k\le\beta_\infty N_h^k$ give $N_h^{k+1}\le(1+\Delta t\beta_\infty)N_h^k$, hence $N_h^k\le e^{\beta_\infty T}N_h^0$. Since $N_h^0\le\|n_0\|_1+\epsilon_0$ (test the initial BL defect with $\phi\equiv1$), the sum of the initial cohort masses and all inserted newborn masses $\sum_{j<k}\Delta t B_h^j$ is at most $C_T(\|n_0\|_1+\epsilon_0)$. Thus the sum of all cohort survival-weight errors is at most $C_T\Delta t(\|n_0\|_1+\epsilon_0)$. [F3, F4, L1, step 1.1, algebra]

old: 1.1 For real addition and subtraction, every exact pair value lies between the endpoint formulas. For multiplication, fixing one variable makes the product affine in the other, so a minimum or maximum over a rectangle is attained at a corner. Reciprocal is monotone on either interval avoiding zero, and square root is monotone on $[0,\infty)$. Thus the exact ranges lie in the displayed pre-rounding intervals. Each computed lower endpoint is no greater than the exact lower endpoint and each upper endpoint is no smaller than the exact upper endpoint by [L2]; square-root endpoint bounds follow from [L3]. For complex rectangles, component addition and multiplication preserve the exact component formulas. If a rectangle excludes zero, at least one coordinate interval omits zero, so its squared interval has positive lower endpoint; component interval operations then enclose the exact reciprocal and quotient. [given, L1, L2, L3, algebra]

1.2 For a ball $B(c,r)$, the coordinate projection intervals in [L1] contain each real and imaginary component. By [L5]–[L6], $|i\Im z|=|\Im z|$; the complex triangle inequality [L4] therefore gives $|z|=|\Re z+i\Im z|\le|\Re z|+|\Im z|\le M_B$. Also $|z|^2=(\Re z)^2+(\Im z)^2\ge(\Re z)^2=|\Re z|^2$ by [L7]. If $|z|<|\Re z|$, nonnegativity would imply $|z|^2<|\Re z|^2$, a contradiction. Hence $|z|\ge|\Re z|$; the same argument gives $|z|\ge|\Im z|$. Every point of $X_B$ and $Y_B$ has absolute value at least its corresponding $d$ value, so $|z|\ge m_B$. For $z\in B_1,w\in B_2$, [L4] gives $|z\pm w|\le M_{B_1}+M_{B_2}$ and $|zw|\le M_{B_1}M_{B_2}$. If $m_{B_2}>0$, then $|w|\ge m_{B_2}$ and $|z/w|\le M_{B_1}/m_{B_2}$. Upward radius rounding in [L1] preserves these bounds, proving soundness of all finite ball results. [given, L1, L4, L5, L6, L7, algebra]

1.3 Inclusion of balls implies inclusion of each coordinate projection interval. Therefore $M_B$ cannot decrease and $m_B$ cannot increase as an input ball enlarges. The ball addition, subtraction and multiplication radii in [L1] are consequently nondecreasing. If both divisor results are finite, the larger divisor ball has positive $m_B$ and the smaller one has at least as large an $m_B$; the quotient radius therefore cannot decrease when either ball is enlarged. For intervals and rectangles, the exact endpoint hulls and their downward/upward roundings preserve inclusion, so their finite extensions are isotone as well; for square root, [L3] gives monotonicity of the computed endpoint maps. If a domain restriction is lost, the operation returns its stated non-finite status. [step 1.1, step 1.2, L1, L2, L3, algebra]

Induct along this order: if each predecessor of an operation node contains its exact value, steps 1.1–1.3 show that the operation enclosure contains the node's exact value. The induction covers every node, including the root, for every admissible assignment. [L1, L5, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, induction, construct] ∎

3.2 For every two coordinates $Z_a,Z_b$, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $\mathbb E|Z_aZ_b|<\infty$. Each product is the same measurable function of every iid row; [F4] gives independence and the common row law gives identical distributions. Thus [F5] gives convergence in probability of the sample means of all finitely many products $Z_aZ_b$. Step 2.1 gives convergence of the row means. Expanding the sample covariance around those means by [F11] proves $\widehat\Sigma\to\Sigma$ in probability. Continuity of the derivative of $g$ near $\eta$ then gives $\widehat J\widehat\Sigma\widehat J^{\mathsf T}\to J\Sigma J^{\mathsf T}$ in probability. Since the algorithm returns $M_n=\widehat J\widehat\Sigma\widehat J^{\mathsf T}/n$, this proves the stated scaled covariance convergence. An arbitrary fixed finite extension on the zero-status event preserves convergence in probability because that event has probability tending to zero by step 2.1. The argument does not claim an unbiased ratio. [F1, F4, F5, F7, F8, F11, step 1.1, step 2.1, given, algebra]

4.1 In each row [F1] evaluates $f(X)$ once and reuses it in every hybrid expression, evaluates the $d$ first-order and $d$ total-effect hybrids, and evaluates the four additional values $f(U),f(V),f(W),f(W')$. old: 1.1 For an exponential input interval, the fixed scale puts every scaled point in $[-1/2,1/2]$. The point bound [L3] with $|u|$ replaced by the interval's largest absolute endpoint gives a uniform tail enclosure. The truncated polynomial interval-evaluates every point by [L2]. The tail radius increases with the largest absolute input, and each repeated interval square preserves inclusion by [L2]. To justify the scaling identity, put $d=2^s$. Repeated applications of [L6] to the absolutely convergent series for $\exp u$ show that the coefficient of $u^k$ in $(\exp u)^d$ is $$\sum_{n_1+\cdots+n_d=k}\frac1{n_1!\cdots n_d!} =\frac{d^k}{k!},$$ where the equality is the multinomial theorem. Thus $(\exp u)^d=\exp(du)$; set $u=x/d$. Each interval squaring preserves the resulting enclosure by [L2]. [given, L1, L2, L3, L6, algebra]

1.2 On each positive logarithm bin, every $y$ maps to $v=(y-1)/(y+1)\in[0,1/3]$. The interval series and uniform tail from [L3] contain $\ln y$; [L3] also proves the exact logarithm scaling identity used by the algorithm. Each interval transform and sum preserves inclusion by [L2]. The fixed bin partition ensures that enlarging the input only enlarges the intersection with each bin, so its interval-series enclosure and the final hull also enlarge. The arctangent transformations follow from [L5]; on each fixed branch the rational interval maps and fixed series are isotone, and the tail radius is nondecreasing in the largest absolute transformed endpoint. [step 1.1, given, L1, L2, L3, L5, algebra]

2.1 The outward cell interval built from $P_N$ contains each exact canonical cell, since $\pi\in P_N$; thus its intersection hull $X_k$ contains every input point assigned to that cell, and $X_k-kP_N/2$ contains the exact residual $r=x-k\pi/2$. The algorithm certifies this residual inside the Taylor range. By [L4], exact sine and cosine values are the stated signed swaps of $\sin r$ and $\cos r$. The polynomial interval evaluation contains each truncated value by [L2], and adding the symmetric tail interval from [L4] contains the omitted remainder. Taking the hull over all intersected cells therefore contains the full range. If the interval width is at least $2\pi$, [L4] gives the safe range $[-1,1]$. For nested inputs, each fixed canonical cell intersection enlarges and its fixed-term interval evaluation is isotone by [L2]; the hull is therefore nested on the reduced branch. Exact rational interval polynomial and tail operations are inclusion-isotone, and the final directed endpoint conversions are nondecreasing. Intersecting with $[-1,1]$ preserves containment and nesting, and ensures that the wide-input $[-1,1]$ return contains every narrower finite result. [given, L1, L2, L4, algebra]

2.2 Tangent is defined only where cosine is nonzero. On a piece whose cosine enclosure excludes zero, division is sound by [L2] and contains every $\sin x/\cos x$. If cosine may vanish, the algorithm returns a split or non-finite status, so no unsound finite value is reported. The same argument applies to square root using the bisection supplier in [L2]. [step 2.1, L1, L2]

3.1 Evaluate the finite expression DAG in topological order. Every primitive node encloses its exact value by steps 1.1–2.2; induction over the finite node order then encloses every exact intermediate and every requested output range. Each primitive's canonical partition and fixed truncation are nested on common finite branches, so the same induction preserves inclusion for nested inputs evaluated with the same format and truncation index. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 2.2, induction] ∎

old: 1.1 Fix $h=\tau/m\le h_0$, let $N$ be the least integer with $Nh\ge T$, and put $T_h=Nh\le T+\eta$. Run the algorithm through $T_h$ and call its stored interpolant $\widehat y_h$. Convex interpolation and [A1] give $\|\widehat y_h(t)\|_2\le R$. Extend it constantly just beyond each endpoint for local ODE neighborhoods of time radius less than $\min\{\rho,\tau\}$. Define $F_h(t,x)=f(t,x,\widehat y_h(t-\tau))$ for $0\le t\le T_h$. It is continuous and $L_s$-Lipschitz in $x$. By [F3], $\|F_h(t,0)\|_2\le Q+L_sR$. Local solutions of $z'=F_h(t,z)$ therefore obey $\|z(t)\|_2\le\|\phi(0)\|_2+(Q+L_sR)t+L_s\int_0^t\|z(s)\|_2ds$. The vector integral norm bound [F5] and triangle inequality [F12] justify this estimate. For $t\le T+\eta$, replace the first two terms by the constant $A=\|\phi(0)\|_2+(Q+L_sR)(T+\eta)$ and apply [F10]; this gives $\|z(t)\|_2\le Ae^{L_s(T+\eta)}=R_z$. On the compact tube of radius $R_*$ the field is bounded by $M_f$, so [F8] continues each local solution by a common positive short-time amount while it remains in that ball. The a priori bound keeps each continuation endpoint within radius $R_z$; finitely many continuations cover $[0,T_h]$. Denote the resulting solution by $z_h$ and set $z_h=\phi$ on $[-\tau,0]$. Since $t_n-\tau=t_{n-m}$ is a stored node, [F2] shows the Euler updates are exactly forward Euler applied to this fixed ODE. [F2, F3, F5, F4, F8, F10, F12, A1, given, construct]

1.2 The auxiliary path and the Euler states lie in the radius-$R_*$ tube, and $\|z_h'(t)\|_2\le M_f$. On positive-time cells, each slope of $\widehat y_h$ is an Euler right-hand side bounded by $M_f$; on history cells, [F4] and [F5] bound its slope by $\sup\|\phi'\|_2$. Thus $\widehat y_h$ is $S$-Lipschitz on $[-\tau,T_h]$. [F2, F4, F5, given, step 1.1, algebra]

2.1 The Euler map for the fixed ODE is $\Psi_{h,n}(x)=x+hF_h(t_n,x)$. By [F3] and the triangle inequality [F12] it satisfies $\|\Psi_{h,n}(x)-\Psi_{h,n}(\widetilde x)\|_2\le (1+L_sh)\|x-\widetilde x\|_2$. For $s\in[t_n,t_{n+1}]$, [F3], the time bound, and step 1.2 give $$\|F_h(s,z_h(s))-F_h(t_n,z_h(t_n))\|_2 \le (L_t+L_s(M_f+S))(s-t_n).$$ By [F4], the exact increment is the integral of $F_h(s,z_h(s))$; integrating this estimate and using [F5] gives exact-start local defect at most $C_{\rm loc}h^2$ by [F11] and [F12]. Apply [F9] on the uniform grid of length $T_h$, with initial error zero. Since $T_h\le T+\eta$, it gives $$\max_{0\le n\le N}\|Y_n-z_h(t_n)\|_2\le C_{\rm ode}h.$$ [F3, F4, F5, F9, F11, F12, A1, given, step 1.2, algebra]

2.2 On a solution cell, the nodal error bound proved in the preceding step contributes at most $C_{\rm ode}h$ by the triangle inequality [F12]. The interpolant of the two exact $z_h$ endpoints differs from $z_h(t)$ by at most $M_fh/2$: if $\lambda=(t-t_n)/h$, the endpoint-increment estimate is $2\lambda(1-\lambda)M_fh\le M_fh/2$. Hence $\|\widehat y_h(t)-z_h(t)\|_2\le(C_{\rm ode}+M_f/2)h$. On history cells, [F6] gives error at most $M_\phi h^2/8\le (M_\phi h_0/8)h$. Therefore $$\sup_{-\tau\le t\le T_h}\|\widehat y_h(t)-z_h(t)\|_2\le C_{\rm hist}h.$$ [F2, F6, F12, given, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

3.1 Let $u(t)=\|z_h(t)-y(t)\|_2$ for $-\tau\le t\le T_h$. It is zero on the history. Subtract the integral equations for $z_h$ and $y$ using [F1] and [F4], then use [F3] and bound $\|\widehat y_h(t-\tau)-y(t-\tau)\|_2$ by $C_{\rm hist}h+u(t-\tau)$ using step 2.2. This yields $$u(t)\le\int_0^t\bigl(L_sC_{\rm hist}h+L_s(u(s)+u(s-\tau))\bigr)ds.$$ Apply [F7] with $H=0$ and constant forcing $q=L_sC_{\rm hist}h$ to obtain $\sup_{0\le t\le T_h}u(t)\le L_sC_{\rm hist}h(T+\eta)e^{2L_s(T+\eta)}$. The triangle inequality and the interpolation bound from step 2.2 give the claimed estimate on $[-\tau,T]$ by [F12]. [F1, F3, F4, F7, F12, given, step 1.1, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

2.2 On $I_k=[k\tau,\min\{(k+1)\tau,T\}]$, define the known delayed input $z_k(t)=y(t-\tau)$ from the history and already constructed pieces. Choose a compact time neighborhood $U_0\subset U$ of $[0,T]$ and put $Q_*:=\sup_{t\in U_0}\|f(t,0,0)\|_2$; this is finite by [F4] applied to the continuous norm of $f(t,0,0)$. Choose a common $\delta>0$ inside the time-domain margin with $L\delta<1$ and $\delta M_*\le1$. [F2] gives a unique local solution from each current endpoint, and finitely many subintervals of length at most $\delta$ cover $I_k$; the bound in step 2.1 keeps every endpoint in the required ball. old: 1.1 Let $\bar\delta_\varepsilon:= \min\{c_\delta\varepsilon,\Delta_{max}\}$. Every radius during a pre-target trial is at least $$r_\varepsilon=\min\{\Delta_0,\gamma_{dec}\bar\delta_\varepsilon\}>0.$$ Indeed, this holds initially. If a trial is rejected, [F3] implies its radius exceeded $\bar\delta_\varepsilon$, since at or below that threshold the ratio is at least $\eta_2$; after multiplication by $\gamma_{dec}$ the new radius is greater than $\gamma_{dec}\bar\delta_\varepsilon$. An accepted update does not decrease the radius. Induction proves the bound. [given, A1, A2, F1, F3, induction, algebra]

1.2 If the target were never reached, every rejection block would be finite: an infinite block would multiply a fixed radius by $\gamma_{dec}^j\to0$ by [F8], eventually making $\Delta\le\bar\delta_\varepsilon$, where [F3] forbids rejection. Thus an infinite pre-target run would contain infinitely many accepted trials. For any accepted trial its starting gradient norm $a$ exceeds $\varepsilon$. From step 1.1, $\Delta_k\ge r_\varepsilon\ge c_R\varepsilon$, because $\varepsilon\le1$ and $$\min\{c_\delta\varepsilon,\Delta_{max}\} \ge\varepsilon\min\{c_\delta,\Delta_{max}\}.$$ Since $\Delta_0\ge\varepsilon\Delta_0$, taking the minimum with $\Delta_0$ in the definition of $r_\varepsilon$ gives $r_\varepsilon\ge c_R\varepsilon$. Also $a/\|B_k\|_2\ge\varepsilon/M_B$, with the stated infinity convention if $M_B=0$. Hence $$\min\{\Delta_k,a/\|B_k\|_2\}\ge c_P\varepsilon.$$ By [F1] and [F2], the predicted reduction is at least $\tfrac12\theta_Cc_P\varepsilon^2$. Acceptance gives actual decrease at least $\eta_1$ times this amount, namely $c_S\varepsilon^2$. If the target were never reached, after $m$ accepted trials the objective would be at most $f(x_0)-m c_S\varepsilon^2$. By [F7] choose an integer $m>(f(x_0)-f_{inf})/(c_S\varepsilon^2)$; this contradicts [A3]. Therefore the target is reached after finitely many accepted trials. Summing their decreases gives $N_s c_S\varepsilon^2\le f(x_0)-f_{inf}$, the claimed successful-step bound. [given, A1, A2, A3, F1, F2, F3, F7, F8, step 1.1, choose, assume-contra, discharge-contradiction, algebra]

2.1 Let $\Delta_T$ be the radius after the accepted trial that first reaches the target. Each rejected trial multiplies the radius by $\gamma_{dec}$; each accepted update multiplies it by some $r_j\in[1,\gamma_{inc}]$. Therefore $$\Delta_T=\Delta_0\gamma_{dec}^{N_u}\prod_{j=1}^{N_s}r_j.$$ Step 1.1 gives $\Delta_T\ge r_\varepsilon$.
